subject: Religious and Moral Education
source: RELIGIOUS AND MORAL EDUCATION CURRICULUM FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS (BASIC I - 6), September 2019
teacher_guidance: Read questions aloud where needed. Accept verbal, drawn, and demonstrative answers. Basic 1 indicators BI. 4.1.1. (printed with a missing digit) and the other family/community indicators are covered with exact fidelity to the curriculum exemplars.

indicators.strand: Religious Practices and their Moral Implications
indicators.sub_strand: Religious Festivals in the Three Major Religions in Ghana

skills.description: Identify and name festivals celebrated by Christians (Christmas, Easter), Muslims (Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Adha), and Traditionalists (Odwira, Damba, Homowo, Hogbetsotso, Fetu Afahye).
Describe activities and meanings of religious festivals (sharing food, reconciliation, family gathering).
Explain values of unity, sharing, and reconciliation promoted during religious festivals.

misconceptions: Confusing Christmas with Easter (birth vs. death and resurrection of Jesus)
Thinking festivals are only for eating and drinking without moral purpose
Confusing which festival belongs to which of the three religions

questions.stem: Which festival celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ among Christians?
hints: It is celebrated on 25th December.
questions.explanation: Christmas is the Christian festival commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing an Islamic festival with a Christian festival
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing a traditional festival with a Christian festival
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing a traditional/cultural festival with a Christian festival

questions.stem: Which festival is celebrated by Muslims at the end of the fasting month of Ramadan?
hints: It marks the breaking of the fast.
questions.explanation: Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated by Muslims to mark the end of Ramadan.

distractor_misconceptions.0: Confusing a Christian festival with an Islamic festival
distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing Easter with an Islamic feast
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing an Akan traditional festival with an Islamic celebration

questions.stem: Which of these is a traditional festival celebrated in Ghana?
hints: It is celebrated by the Ga people of Accra.
questions.explanation: Homowo is an African Traditional festival listed in the curriculum.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing a Christian feast with traditional festival
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing a Christian holy day with traditional festival

questions.stem: Which Christian festival remembers the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ?
hints: It comes with Good Friday and Easter Sunday.
questions.explanation: Easter is the Christian festival marking the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

questions.stem: Which of these is an Islamic feast of sacrifice?
hints: It commemorates Prophet Ibrahim's sacrifice.
questions.explanation: Eid-ul-Adha is the Islamic festival of sacrifice.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing an Ewe traditional festival with an Islamic festival
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing a Christian festival with an Islamic festival
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing a Fante traditional festival with an Islamic festival

questions.stem: Odwira, Homowo, Hogbetsotso, and Fetu Afahye are festivals belonging to which religion?
hints: These are indigenous Ghanaian community festivals.
questions.explanation: These festivals belong to African Traditional Religion (ATR) in Ghana.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Attributing Ghanaian traditional festivals to Christianity
distractor_misconceptions.2: Attributing Ghanaian traditional festivals to Islam

questions.stem: Name two traditional festivals listed in our RME curriculum.
hints: Think of Odwira, Damba, Homowo, Hogbetsotso, or Fetu Afahye.
questions.explanation: Learners recall any two traditional festivals explicitly named in the curriculum.

criteria.description: Names two valid traditional festivals from the curriculum list.

questions.stem: What special activity do Muslims do during Eid celebrations?
options: Share food and meat with neighbours and the poor
hints: Festivals are times of kindness and sharing.
questions.explanation: Sharing meals, charity, and caring for neighbours are central to Eid celebrations.

distractor_misconceptions.3: Thinking festivals mean neglecting religious duties

questions.stem: Describe one thing families do together when celebrating Christmas in Ghana.
hints: Think about special food, church visits, or family gatherings.
questions.explanation: Learners describe positive family practices such as attending church services and sharing meals.

criteria.description: Mentions a positive family activity during Christmas (e.g. going to church, sharing meals).
Explains that it brings joy to the family.

questions.stem: What does the Ga festival 'Homowo' mean in English?
hints: It means hooting at hunger.
questions.explanation: Homowo means 'hooting at hunger', remembering how the ancestors overcame a period of severe famine.

criteria.description: Explains 'hooting at hunger' or triumph over famine.

questions.stem: During traditional festivals like Odwira and Hogbetsotso, chiefs and people gather to:
options: Settle disputes and clean the community
hints: Traditional festivals bring unity, cleansing, and peace.
questions.explanation: Traditional festivals are times for community reconciliation, purification, and development.

questions.stem: Your Muslim friend invites you for rice and meat during Eid. What polite response should you give?
hints: Say thank you and wish them a blessed Eid.
questions.explanation: Polite greetings show interfaith respect and friendship.

criteria.description: Demonstrates gratitude and courtesy.
Shows interfaith friendship and respect.

questions.stem: Draw people celebrating a religious festival in your town or village. Tell your teacher which festival it is.
hints: Draw people in nice clothes sharing food or dancing.
questions.explanation: Learners visually express festival celebrations and identify the event.

criteria.description: Depicts a festive gathering.
Names the festival and states its religion correctly.

questions.stem: Explain why religious festivals are good times for people who have quarreled to make peace.
hints: Festivals teach reconciliation and forgiveness.
questions.explanation: Religious festivals remind us to forgive, share love, and live together peacefully.

criteria.description: Mentions reconciliation or forgiving one another.
Connects it to religious teachings of love and unity.

questions.stem: Which of these values is promoted by ALL religious festivals in Ghana?
hints: Festivals unite people.
questions.explanation: Togetherness, unity, and reconciliation are core values of all religious festivals.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Thinking festivals promote negative moral qualities
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing celebration with destructive waste and quarrels

questions.stem: How does sharing food during festivals help needy and hungry people in the community?
hints: It gives them a good meal and shows love.
questions.explanation: Sharing festival meals ensures everyone feels included, cared for, and fed.

criteria.description: Explains that the needy get food and joy.
Links sharing to kindness and community love.

questions.stem: Act out two neighbours who had a misunderstanding shaking hands and making peace on a festival day.
hints: Show greeting, forgiving, and sharing a smile.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates reconciliation in a practical role-play.

criteria.description: Demonstrates resolving a conflict peacefully.
Shows forgiveness and warm friendship.

questions.stem: A child says, 'Because I am a Christian, I should throw away food given to me by my Muslim or Traditional neighbour during their festival.' Is this right? Explain using our RME values.
hints: Think about love, sharing, and good neighbourliness.
questions.explanation: We should receive gifts politely and appreciate kindness, fostering peaceful living among religions.

criteria.description: States that rejecting or wasting food rudely is wrong.
Explains that accepting kind gestures with respect fosters peace and unity.

questions.stem: Give two reasons why families travel long distances to attend festivals in their hometowns.
hints: Think about family reunion and helping the community.
questions.explanation: People travel to see relatives, reunite with extended families, and contribute to local community projects.

criteria.description: Mentions family reunions and seeing relatives.
Mentions community unity, planning development, or honouring heritage.

questions.stem: Describe how festivals make Ghana a peaceful and united nation.
hints: People celebrate together and respect each other.
questions.explanation: Festivals celebrate cultural and religious identity while encouraging mutual respect and peaceful coexistence.

criteria.description: Mentions unity and friendship across different groups.
Mentions mutual appreciation of Ghana's cultural and religious heritage.

indicators.objective: Narrate the stories of the birth of religious leaders.
indicators.content_standard_as_printed: BI. 3.1.1. Narrate the birth stories of the leaders of the three main religions
indicators.sub_strand: Birth of the Leaders of the three Major Religions in Ghana

skills.description: Identify the leaders of the three main religions in Ghana (Jesus Christ for Christianity, Holy Prophet Muhammad for Islam, and traditional leaders/priests/founders like Okomfo Anokye).
Recall key details of birth narratives of religious leaders as taught in primary RME.
Dramatise or explain lessons of patience, humility, and caring from the birth of religious leaders.

misconceptions: Confusing the birthplaces or mothers of Jesus and Prophet Muhammad
Thinking Traditional religion has no historical or spiritual founders/leaders
Believing religious leaders were born into wealthy royal palaces with modern luxuries

questions.stem: Who is the religious leader whose birth is celebrated at Christmas by Christians?
hints: He was born in Bethlehem.
questions.explanation: Jesus Christ is the leader of Christianity whose birth is celebrated at Christmas.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing the Islamic prophet with the Christian leader
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing a traditional priest with the Christian leader
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing an ancestral leader with Jesus Christ

questions.stem: Who is the Holy Prophet and leader of Islam?
hints: He was born in Makkah (Mecca).
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the Holy Prophet and leader of Islam.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing the Christian leader with the Islamic Prophet
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing an Akan traditional leader with the Islamic Prophet
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing an earlier prophet with the leader of Islam

questions.stem: Name the famous traditional priest associated with the Golden Stool of the Ashanti Kingdom.
hints: He was a famous spiritual leader in Ghanaian history.
questions.explanation: Okomfo Anokye is a prominent traditional religious and spiritual leader in Ghana.
questions.misconception: Assuming traditional religion has no well-known leaders or priests

questions.stem: In which town was Jesus Christ born?
hints: It is known as the city of David in Judea.
questions.explanation: According to the Christian birth narrative, Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing a Ghanaian city with the biblical birthplace
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing the birthplace of Prophet Muhammad with that of Jesus
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing modern capital of Ghana with ancient Bethlehem

questions.stem: In which holy city was Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.) born?
hints: It is the city where the Ka'bah is located.
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.) was born in Makkah.

distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing the birthplace of Jesus with that of Prophet Muhammad

questions.stem: Who was the mother of Jesus Christ?
hints: She was visited by Angel Gabriel.
questions.explanation: Mary (Maryam) is the mother of Jesus Christ.

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing the mother of Prophet Muhammad with the mother of Jesus
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing Samuel's mother with Jesus' mother
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing Abraham's wife with Jesus' mother

questions.stem: Who was the mother of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.)?
hints: Her name was Amina bint Wahb.
questions.explanation: Amina was the mother of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.).

distractor_misconceptions.1: Confusing the mother of Jesus with the mother of Prophet Muhammad
distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing the Prophet's first wife with his mother
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing another wife with his mother

questions.stem: Tell where baby Jesus was laid when he was born, and why.
hints: Think of a manger in a stable because there was no room in the inn.
questions.explanation: He was laid in a manger (an animal feeding trough) because there was no room for them in the inn.

criteria.description: Mentions that he was laid in a manger/stable.
Explains there was no room in the inn or guest house.

questions.stem: What sad event happened before Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.) was born?
hints: Think of his father, Abdullah.
questions.explanation: His father, Abdullah, passed away before he was born, so he was born an orphan.

criteria.description: Mentions that his father passed away before his birth (he was an orphan).

questions.stem: Who visited baby Jesus following a bright star in the East?
hints: They brought gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
questions.explanation: The Wise Men (Magi) followed the star to bring gifts to baby Jesus.

distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing later disciples with birth visitors
distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing Old Testament figures with Christmas narrative

questions.stem: What special signs or traditional stories are told in our communities about the births of great traditional leaders or priests?
hints: Think of unusual events or prophecies spoken by elders.
questions.explanation: Traditional narratives often speak of elders receiving signs, dreams, or prophecies predicting that the child would be a great leader.

criteria.description: Mentions a dream, prophecy, or special sign reported by elders.

questions.stem: What gifts did the Wise Men present to baby Jesus?
hints: Three precious gifts were given.
questions.explanation: The Wise Men presented gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

questions.stem: In small groups, dramatise the story of Mary, Joseph, and the birth of baby Jesus in Bethlehem.
hints: Show gentle care for the baby in the manger.
questions.explanation: Learners role-play Mary, Joseph, and visitors with reverence and gentleness.

criteria.description: Portrays the nativity scene respectfully.
Shows care for the newborn infant.

questions.stem: What does the humble birth of Jesus in a manger teach us about being proud or humble?
hints: God chose a simple, humble place.
questions.explanation: It teaches us humility, showing that greatness does not require boasting or luxury.

criteria.description: Explains that it teaches humility and simplicity.
Notes that we should not look down on simple places or people.

questions.stem: Draw the stable or manger where baby Jesus was born, or draw a scene from the birth of a religious leader. Explain your picture.
hints: Draw a small crib or manger with stars above.
questions.explanation: Learners illustrate a birth scene and explain its meaning to the teacher.

criteria.description: Draws an appropriate birth scene.
Accurately explains the key elements of the drawing.

questions.stem: Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W.) was cared for with deep love by his mother Amina and grandfather Abdul Muttalib. What does this teach families today?
hints: Think about caring for orphans and children.
questions.explanation: It teaches family members to care tenderly for children, especially those who lose a parent.

criteria.description: Mentions caring for orphans and young children.
Connects it to family responsibility and love.

questions.stem: A child says, 'Only children born to rich families can become good and great leaders.' Use the birth of Jesus or Prophet Muhammad to correct this idea.
hints: Both were born in very simple or humble circumstances.
questions.explanation: Both leaders were born in modest, humble settings, proving that God can make any child a great leader regardless of wealth.

criteria.description: Points out that Jesus or Muhammad was born in humble/simple conditions.
Concludes that honesty and goodness, not wealth, make a great leader.

questions.stem: Dramatise how neighbours and relatives in Ghana visit a newborn baby with blessings, songs, and small gifts, just as people visited religious leaders at their birth.
hints: Show elders praying and welcoming the child.
questions.explanation: Connects the historic birth narratives to Ghanaian child-welcoming and naming traditions.

criteria.description: Demonstrates respectful cultural welcoming of a newborn.
Connects the joy of new birth to religious stories.

questions.stem: Compare how both Christian and Islamic birth stories show God's special care and protection over the leaders when they were babies.
hints: Think of angels, stars, and loving family care.
questions.explanation: Both traditions emphasize divine protection through family, dreams, or messengers guiding the infant safely.

criteria.description: Identifies divine care and protection in the Christian story.
Identifies divine care and protection in the Islamic story.
Notes that God cares for all children.

questions.stem: Tell what moral values (such as love, patience, and humility) we should practice in school after learning about the birth of religious leaders.
hints: Choose two moral values and give an example for each.
questions.explanation: Learners apply the values of humility and caring to everyday school life.

criteria.description: Names two relevant values (e.g. humility, patience, love).
Provides practical classroom examples for both.

uncertain: Narratives for traditional leaders depend on local Ghanaian oral accounts; the exemplars specifically mandate stories of the birth of ATR leaders alongside Christian and Islamic leaders.

indicators.objective: Identify the role of the individual members of the family.
indicators.content_standard_as_printed: BI. 4.1.1. Show an appreciation of the roles of the family and community in their daily lives

skills.description: Identify roles of parents in the family (provision of shelter, food, security, and education).
Identify roles of children in the family (running errands, performing house chores, showing respect and obedience).
Role-play and explain the importance of cooperation, love, and togetherness in the family.

misconceptions: Thinking children have no duties or responsibilities at home
Believing parents only provide food and nothing else
Assuming chores are a punishment rather than helpful cooperation

questions.stem: Which of these is a major duty of parents to their children according to our lesson?
options: Telling children not to attend school
hints: Parents provide what children need to grow safely.
questions.explanation: Parents have the responsibility of providing food, shelter, security, and education.

questions.stem: When parents provide a safe house for the family to sleep in, what are they providing?
hints: A house protects from rain and sun.
questions.explanation: A safe house provides shelter for the family.

distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing home with a commercial place

questions.stem: Parents pay school fees and buy books. Which need are they providing?
hints: Think about going to school and learning.
questions.explanation: Providing books, uniforms, and schooling is providing education.
questions.misconception: Thinking education is not a parental responsibility

questions.stem: What is one helpful chore a Basic 1 child can do at home?
hints: Choose a safe and light task for a young child.
questions.explanation: Sweeping is a safe and helpful chore suitable for a young child.

questions.stem: When a parent asks a child to fetch water or bring a cup, what is the child doing?
options: Washing a car on the highway
hints: It is a small task done to help.
questions.explanation: Carrying out small helpful instructions for parents is running an errand.

distractor_misconceptions.3: Confusing home tasks with sleeping in class

questions.stem: When children listen to and obey their parents, what moral value are they showing?
hints: It starts with 'r' or 'o'.
questions.explanation: Listening and following good instructions demonstrates respect and obedience.

questions.stem: Name two chores you can do at home to help your parents or guardians.
hints: Think of sweeping, packing toys, wiping tables, or fetching water.
questions.explanation: Learners state two safe, age-appropriate home chores.

criteria.description: Names two safe and realistic chores for a child.

questions.stem: Protecting children from danger and harm is which role of parents?
hints: Security means keeping someone safe.
questions.explanation: Keeping children safe from harm is providing security.

questions.stem: Explain why parents work hard every day to earn money for the family.
hints: Think of buying food, clothes, and paying school fees.
questions.explanation: Parents work to provide food, shelter, clothes, healthcare, and education for their family.

criteria.description: Mentions providing food, shelter, or education.
Connects work to caring for family needs.

questions.stem: Your mother calls you to bring her drinking water while you are playing. What should you do?
hints: Pause your play and respond politely.
questions.explanation: Stop play, answer politely, and run the errand promptly.

criteria.description: States answering politely and running the errand.
Shows respect and willingness to help.

questions.stem: What happens in a home when parents and children help each other with love and respect?
options: The home is peaceful, happy, and united
hints: Cooperation brings joy and peace.
questions.explanation: Cooperation and love produce a peaceful, happy, and orderly home.

distractor_misconceptions.3: Thinking mutual help causes children to flee

questions.stem: Role-play with a partner: One plays the father or mother coming home tired, and the other plays a child greeting them politely and offering water.
hints: Show warm greetings and serving water.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates respect, care, and good manners in the family.

criteria.description: Demonstrates respectful greeting.
Offers help or water cheerfully.

questions.stem: Kofi says, 'I am only a child, so I should throw my rubbish on the floor and let my mother sweep it.' Why is Kofi wrong?
hints: Everyone should keep the house tidy.
questions.explanation: Children should be responsible by putting rubbish in the bin and keeping their home clean.

criteria.description: Explains that children must help keep the home clean.
Points out that dumping rubbish creates unfair work for parents.

questions.stem: Draw yourself doing a helpful chore at home with your family. Tell your teacher what chore you drew.
hints: Draw yourself sweeping, washing plates, or watering plants.
questions.explanation: Learners visually illustrate family chores and explain their helpful contribution.

criteria.description: Draws a domestic chore.
Explains how it helps the family.

questions.stem: Mention three things your parents provide for you, and tell why you are grateful to them.
hints: Food, clothes, shelter, school items.
questions.explanation: Learners identify three provisions and express appreciation.

criteria.description: Accurately lists three parental provisions.
Expresses genuine gratitude and appreciation.

questions.stem: In groups of three, act out a family preparing an evening meal together (one washing vegetables, one setting the table, one cooking).
hints: Show team effort in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates teamwork and division of labour in the household.

criteria.description: Demonstrates cooperative domestic work.
Shows joy and mutual respect among family members.

questions.stem: How does greeting your parents and elders every morning show respect in a Ghanaian home?
hints: Greetings show love and honour.
questions.explanation: Morning greetings honour parents, show good training, and invite blessings.

criteria.description: Explains that greetings show honour and good manners.
Connects it to Ghanaian cultural identity and love.

questions.stem: If an elder brother and sister have to share one toy or book, how should they handle it without quarreling?
hints: Think about taking turns and sharing.
questions.explanation: They should share, take turns, and speak gently with love.

criteria.description: Suggests taking turns and sharing fairly.
Explains that patience avoids fighting and maintains love.

questions.stem: Why is the family called the first and most important school for every child?
hints: Where do we learn to talk, greet, and behave well?
questions.explanation: The family is where we first learn love, moral values, respect, and language before starting formal school.

criteria.description: Mentions learning moral values, respect, and manners at home.
Notes that parents are a child's first teachers.

questions.stem: Compose a short pledge or message of love to your family promising to be obedient, helpful, and hardworking.
hints: Speak from your heart about helping at home.
questions.explanation: Learners express commitment to family values and responsible childhood conduct.

criteria.description: Promises obedience, help with chores, or dedication to study.
Expresses love and appreciation for family members.

uncertain: The indicator code is printed as 'BI. 4.1.1.' in the curriculum table (missing the final indicator digit) and is preserved as printed.

indicators.objective: Explain the role of the community in the upbringing of its members.
indicators.content_standard_as_printed: BI. 4.1.1. Show an appreciation of the roles of the family and community in their daily lives

skills.description: Identify ways the community contributes to child upbringing (education, discipline, counselling, security).
Recognise roles of community members (teachers, chiefs, elders, police, health workers) in guiding children.
Explain how children should respect community elders and obey communal safety rules.

misconceptions: Thinking community elders have no right to correct a misbehaving child
Believing only one's biological parents care about a child's safety
Assuming discipline from an elder is done out of hatred rather than love

questions.stem: Who makes up our community?
options: Our neighbours, teachers, chiefs, and friends living together
Only people who live in other countries
Only wild animals in the forest
hints: A community is made of people living in the same area.
questions.explanation: A community consists of people living together, including neighbours, elders, teachers, and leaders.

distractor_misconceptions.2: Confusing distant foreigners with local community

questions.stem: According to an African proverb, who raises a child?
options: It takes a whole village (community) to raise a child
Only a television raises a child
hints: Elders and neighbours all help care for children.
questions.explanation: The famous proverb teaches that the whole community participates in child upbringing.

questions.stem: When an elder gently corrects a child doing something dangerous on the street, what are they giving?
hints: It starts with 'd' or 'c'.
questions.explanation: Community elders help through discipline, advice, and correction to keep children safe.
questions.misconception: Thinking elders correct children out of hatred

questions.stem: Which community worker helps children learn reading, writing, and good morals at school?
hints: Think of who guides you in the classroom.
questions.explanation: Teachers educate children in school and teach good values.

questions.stem: Who protects community members and maintains peace and safety in our towns?
hints: They wear uniforms and protect citizens.
questions.explanation: The police and community leaders protect citizens and ensure law and order.

questions.stem: If an elder in your neighbourhood sees you playing near deep water or fire and tells you to stop, what should you do?
hints: Listen, say thank you, and move to a safe place.
questions.explanation: Children should obey the elder immediately because the correction protects them from danger.

criteria.description: States obeying the elder immediately and moving to safety.
Recognises that the elder is protecting them.

questions.stem: Traditional chiefs and queen mothers help the community by:
options: Maintaining peace, settling disputes, and guiding communal development
hints: Traditional leaders are peacemakers and custodians of culture.
questions.explanation: Chiefs and queen mothers maintain peace, settle disputes, and lead community development.

questions.stem: Name the service provided by hospitals and clinics in the community to keep children strong.
hints: Doctors and nurses take care of your body.
questions.explanation: Hospitals and health centres provide healthcare to treat and prevent sickness.
questions.misconception: Thinking healthcare is not a community service

questions.stem: Mention two ways people in your community help one another during celebrations or clean-up exercises.
hints: Think of communal labour, sweeping streets, or helping at funerals and festivals.
questions.explanation: Learners identify communal labour, street cleaning, or mutual assistance at social gatherings.

criteria.description: Names two cooperative community activities (e.g. communal labour, funerals).

questions.stem: When a child feels confused or troubled, talking to a wise elder, religious leader, or teacher for advice is called:
hints: It means receiving wise guidance.
questions.explanation: Receiving wise advice and guidance from trusted adults is counselling.

questions.stem: How should a well-trained child greet an elder they meet on the community street?
options: Greet them politely with a respectful bow or smile
Insult the elder and run away
Look away and pretend not to see them
hints: Greetings show respect and good upbringing.
questions.explanation: Children should greet community elders politely with respect.

questions.stem: Tell your partner why children should not play on busy roads where cars and motorbikes pass.
hints: Vehicles can knock children down.
questions.explanation: Playing on busy roads exposes children to road accidents and serious injury.

criteria.description: Explains the danger of road accidents and injury.
Connects it to obeying community safety rules.

questions.stem: Role-play with a partner: An elder finds a lost child crying in the market, comforts the child, and helps locate the child's parents.
hints: Show kindness, calm words, and taking the child to safety.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates community members protecting vulnerable children.

criteria.description: Demonstrates elder comforting the child kindly.
Shows taking safe steps to find the child's family.

questions.stem: Kwame says, 'A neighbour has no right to tell me to stop throwing stones at dogs because he is not my biological father.' Explain what Kwame has misunderstood about community life.
hints: Every elder in our community looks out for our safety and good character.
questions.explanation: In Ghanaian culture, all community elders share responsibility for guiding children and preventing bad behaviour.

criteria.description: Explains that community elders are like parents who protect and correct all children.
Notes that throwing stones is cruel and dangerous.

questions.stem: Draw a community helper (such as a teacher, doctor, police officer, or chief) doing good work. Explain your drawing.
hints: Draw someone helping others in town.
questions.explanation: Learners visually depict a community helper and articulate their role.

criteria.description: Draws a recognisable community helper.
Explains the helper's contribution to the community.

questions.stem: Describe how religious leaders (pastors, imams, and traditional priests) help maintain peace in our community.
hints: They preach love, pray for peace, and advise people to forgive.
questions.explanation: Religious leaders teach honesty, love, and forgiveness, and mediate conflicts between neighbours.

criteria.description: Mentions teaching moral values or praying for peace.
Mentions settling misunderstandings between neighbours.

questions.stem: Act out participating in a clean-up exercise in your school or neighbourhood compound by picking up litter and sweeping.
hints: Show picking up plastic waste and putting it in bins.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates practical civic responsibility and communal hygiene.

criteria.description: Shows active participation in cleaning.
Demonstrates teamwork and pride in community cleanliness.

questions.stem: Why is it important for children to know their home address or parents' telephone number when moving around the community?
hints: In case you get separated or need help.
questions.explanation: Knowing contact information allows trusted community helpers or police to reunite lost children with their families quickly and safely.

criteria.description: Explains that it helps adults reconnect lost children with parents.
Connects it to personal safety and security.

questions.stem: Explain how education, discipline, and counselling work together in our community to help children grow into responsible citizens.
hints: Education gives knowledge, discipline corrects mistakes, and counselling gives wise advice.
questions.explanation: Education provides skills, discipline instills self-control and good conduct, and counselling guides emotional and moral decisions.

criteria.description: Explains the role of education (knowledge and skills).
Explains the role of discipline (correcting errors, building self-control).
Explains counselling (wise guidance and encouragement).

questions.stem: Give a short speech thanking your community elders, teachers, and neighbours for loving and protecting children every day.
hints: Mention what they do and express warm gratitude.
questions.explanation: Learners articulate appreciation for communal care, reinforcing core values of respect and gratitude.

criteria.description: Names specific community helpers and their contributions.
